systemStatus.appCPUHelp: 100% means one fully occupied CPU core; uses the application container cgroup, excluding the separate database container.
systemStatus.appStorageHelp: Application file sizes plus PostgreSQL database size (including indexes). Excludes image layers, logs, WAL and backups. This is data size, not the whole filesystem or a disk quota. Storage is sampled at most once a minute without blocking requests.
systemStatus.appGPUHelp: No compute GPU is assigned to this container. GPUs used by remote AI providers are not local vikunja-x usage.
systemStatus.title: Server load
systemStatus.cpuHelp: CPU is the host non-idle time across all logical cores, excluding I/O wait. Guest time is not double counted. Samples use total-time deltas and are independent of container CPU quotas.
systemStatus.diskHelp: Used space on the server filesystem containing vikunja-x data, including all other files on that volume. This deployment uses the server root filesystem; separately mounted disks are not summed.
systemStatus.refreshHelp: 5-second shared server cache; CPU and other counters refresh every 5 seconds while the sidebar and tab are visible. Storage is sampled at most once a minute. Server uptime resets on reboot; vikunja-x uptime resets on application restart.
systemStatus.loadHelp: Load counts runnable and uninterruptible tasks across the host. It is not a percentage; compare sustained load with the logical CPU count. I/O waits can raise load even when CPU usage is low.
systemStatus.hostSource: CPU, memory, load and boot uptime come from explicitly mounted read-only host kernel counters and include all applications. Missing host files stay unavailable. The green badge checks vikunja-x dependencies, not host resource pressure.
systemStatus.memoryHelp: RAM used = host total − host available memory. Available includes reclaimable caches, following the kernel estimate. This covers all applications, not only vikunja-x.

modelConfig.title: Model capabilities & capacity
modelConfig.help: Each connection describes one model. Use the provider’s published capabilities or enter values for your gateway. Capacity is measured in tokens, not characters. These settings also apply to compaction.
modelConfig.contextHelp: 0 uses known model metadata; otherwise capacity remains unknown. Used to size compaction batches. It is not a spending budget.
modelConfig.outputHelp: 0 uses known model metadata or leaves the provider default unchanged. Anthropic requires an explicit value; unknown models use 128,000 and you can override it. This allowance may include reasoning; it is not a target response length.
modelConfig.inputsHelp: Declare what this upstream model supports. This does not add vision to a text-only model or turn on a separate image-upload feature.
modelConfig.fieldHelp: Automatic uses max_completion_tokens, or max_tokens for the official DeepSeek API. Override only if your gateway requires it.
modelConfig.useListed: Use capabilities from the model directory
modelConfig.saveToResolve: Save to see the server-resolved values and test this configuration.
modelConfig.autoCompactHelp: When the estimated working context reaches the threshold, the assistant summarizes earlier context before the next request. The full conversation, tool records and provider-returned reasoning are kept; only the context sent to the model gets smaller. This does not limit output tokens.
modelConfig.autoCompactTokensHelp: A policy for when to compact, not the model’s capacity. 0 uses 90% of the declared or known context window, lowered if needed to leave room for the maximum output. If the capacity is unknown, a 128,000-token soft trigger is used; it says nothing about the model itself. With a known capacity, a higher value is capped at the context window minus the maximum output.
modelConfig.disableAutoCompactHelp: The assistant will not compact on its own, not even to recover from a context-overflow error, so a long task may stop once the context is full. Manual “Compact context” in the conversation menu remains available.

help.intro: To filter tasks, you can use a query syntax similar to SQL. The available fields for filtering include:

fields.done: Whether the task is completed or not
fields.priority: The priority level of the task (1-5)
fields.percentDone: The percentage of completion for the task (0-100)
fields.dueDate: The due date of the task
fields.startDate: The start date of the task
fields.endDate: The end date of the task

overview.title: Your starting point
overview.text: The workspace brings today's tasks, quick capture and recently opened projects together. Use the sidebar for everything else. On phones, the guide opens the sidebar when needed.

projects.title: Organize work into projects
projects.text: Create a project here, then add its tasks. Projects support list, kanban, table and Gantt views so you can organize the same work in different ways.

addTask.title: Add a task quickly
addTask.text: Type a task here and choose its project when asked. Open a task to add details, priority, reminders, assignees and dates. The guide will not create a sample task.

upcoming.title: Plan dates and time slots
upcoming.text: Upcoming shows tasks by date. Set a due date for a deadline, or start and end times for a time slot. Use a project’s Gantt view to see how scheduled tasks fit together.

teams.title: Work with other accounts
teams.text: Create teams and add members here. Share projects with users or teams from project settings, with read, write or admin access. Shared tasks support assignees and comments.

search.title: Find things quickly
search.text: Use search to find tasks or projects and run quick actions. Press Ctrl+K on Windows/Linux or Command+K on macOS.

assistant.title: Turn words into a plan
assistant.text: The assistant accepts text and audio. First connect your models in Settings → AI & voice. It can look up accessible tasks or make changes according to your chosen mode.

settings.title: Your account and preferences
settings.text: Open the avatar menu for settings. AI & voice connects your models; Public page shares selected schedules with aliases and privacy rules. Private projects are not automatically public.

replay.title: Help is always here
replay.text: Click the question mark or choose Help & guided tours in the avatar menu to replay a tour. Use Back/Next or the left/right arrow keys to change steps. Escape closes the guide.

connections.title: Connect your model provider
connections.text: Configure your provider’s API base URL, key, model ID and protocol here. Include its required version path. The form shows full request and model-list endpoints for troubleshooting.

addConnection.title: Add and test a connection
addConnection.text: Add a connection here. Text supports OpenAI Chat/Responses, Anthropic and Gemini; speech supports OpenAI Transcriptions, OpenAI Chat Audio and Gemini. Fetch models or enter an ID manually, then save before testing.

roles.title: Choose a model for each job
roles.text: Assign separate models to the task assistant, speech recognition and transcript cleanup. The assistant needs tool calling; speech needs audio input. Each role can use a different provider.

saveModels.title: Save, then test
saveModels.text: Save connections and role assignments here. Leave an existing key blank to keep it. Use each connection’s test button after saving. This guide does not save settings or contact your provider.

permissions.title: Choose what AI may do
permissions.text: Choose a scenario beside the composer. Open Scenarios & preferences to see what each mode allows, adjust budgets, and save your own default template. Start with Ask & explore if you only want suggestions.

voice.title: Speak, review, then send
voice.text: Click the microphone to start and stop recording. On touchscreens you can also hold to record and release to transcribe. Voice options contains audio upload and text cleanup. Review the text before sending.

send.title: Describe the result you want
send.text: Write or review your request here, then send it yourself. Check the operation history and resulting tasks. If a request fails, some earlier operations may already have succeeded.

publication.title: A separate page for visitors
publication.text: Check whether your page is published. After publishing, open the public webpage or JSON endpoint for bots here, or take both down. Visitors do not need an account.

hours.title: Set the public time window
hours.text: Set your page address, title, days and available hours. Tasks with start and end times form busy slots; deadlines do not occupy the whole day. Public calculations use Asia/Shanghai time.

privacy.title: Choose what others may see
privacy.text: Only projects added here appear publicly. Show busy times without names, allow titles with aliases, or hide a project completely. Preview first to alias or hide individual tasks. Private names stay unchanged.

customPage.title: Make the page your own
customPage.text: Write Markdown or static HTML. Insert schedules, availability and projects using the template button. A custom body can replace the default panels. Hiding panels does not change the public JSON’s data scope.

preview.title: Preview before publishing
preview.text: Preview shows the visitor-facing result without publishing it. Review names, hidden tasks and time slots. After editing, preview again before publishing. The guide does not preview or change your draft.

publish.title: Publish only when ready
publish.text: Saving a draft keeps it private. Publish this preview updates the webpage and JSON. Published schedules follow live tasks using the last published rules. Hidden or unselected tasks do not count as busy, so public free time may differ from your full calendar.

On: it pauses when a segment reaches its request or operation limit, so you continue it yourself segment by segment; the time limit ends the segment. projectTimeline.explanationSpans: A task with a start date and an end date (or, without an end date, a due date) is scheduled: its project is shown across those days, and separate tasks with a gap between them stay separate spans. Tasks in sub-projects belong to their own project, not the parent.
projectTimeline.explanationDeadlines: A task with only a due date appears as a deadline on that day. It counts toward the project’s tasks, progress and overdue tasks, but never adds scheduled or passed days. A task whose range lies in another year shows only its deadline in this one. Tasks without any dates are counted separately and never get dates assigned.
projectTimeline.explanationElapsed: “Counted as passed” covers scheduled days up to today, or up to the day a task was marked done; days after an early completion are not counted. It is not a record of hours worked.
projectTimeline.explanationProgress: Progress is the current average completion of the project's scheduled tasks in this year (done tasks count as 100%). It is not a history of past progress.

aronaRun.scopeNoteRuntime: The request row covers one model request. Context in use is what the model works with now: measured by the provider, or estimated from its latest report plus what was added since. Cached tokens still occupy context, and it is never a running total. Without a known capacity there is no percentage, and the auto-compaction threshold is only a policy. The turn total is the provider-reported usage of all finished work in this turn (model requests, searches, automatic compactions and subagents), each counted once; the itemized figures are part of it, not additions, and it is not the context size. While a turn runs, work still in progress is shown separately as a provisional figure.
